title: God, are you there?
theme: Trusting God when we cannot understand what is happening, the limits of human understanding, God's presence in suffering, guardian angels, and faith in the unseen.
opening: How much of what is happening around us can we actually see?
prayer: Lord, there is so much I cannot see and so much I do not understand. When Your ways are beyond me, keep me from believing that Your presence is absent simply because I cannot perceive it. Thank You for seeing us completely, for valuing even the smallest among us, and for the angels who behold Your face. Give us faith when answers remain hidden, and help us trust that what we see is not all there is. Amen.
body:
God finally speaks to Job.
After everything Job has suffered, everything he has questioned, and all the times he has wanted God to answer him, God responds from the storm. But He doesn't answer the question Job has been asking. He doesn't explain why any of this happened. Instead, God begins asking Job questions.
“Have you ever in your lifetime commanded the morning?” Where does light dwell? Has Job walked the depths of the sea? Has he seen the gates of death?
The questions seem to grow larger and more impossible as God continues. I kept wondering why God would ask Job things He already knows Job cannot answer. God isn't testing Job's knowledge. He doesn't need to discover what Job knows. And I don't think He is humiliating a man who has already suffered so much.
So what is the point?
Maybe God's questions are themselves part of the answer.
Job has been asking God to explain what has happened to him. He knows his suffering intimately. He knows what he has lost. He knows what his body feels like, what his friends have accused him of, and how desperately he wants to understand why. But Job knows only what he can see.
We, as readers, already know there is more to his story than Job knows. Job never heard the conversation that began it. He didn't see the accuser roaming the earth or challenging the reason for Job's faithfulness. Job experiences the consequences without being allowed to see everything surrounding them.
Then God asks Job questions about an entire creation that also exists beyond Job's understanding.
Where does light come from? What lies in the depths of the sea? What exists beyond the gates of death?
Job cannot answer.
Finally he puts his hand over his mouth. He has spoken, but he will say no more.
At first his response can almost sound like, I am nothing and I have nothing worth saying. But I don't think God is showing Job that he is nothing. God has already shown how much Job matters to Him.
Job is discovering that he is not God.
He can know his own suffering completely and still know very little about everything surrounding it. He can ask God why and still lack the ability to see from God's vantage point.
And God never gives Job the explanation I keep expecting Him to give.
Instead, He gives Job an encounter with Himself.
That makes today's Gospel about the Guardian Angels surprisingly connected to Job.
Jesus tells His disciples not to despise the little ones because “their angels in heaven always look upon the face of my heavenly Father.”
That stopped me.
Job longs to see God. Yesterday he declared that one day his own eyes would see Him. Today God speaks to him from the storm. Job encounters God, but he still does not see everything God sees.
And then Jesus tells us there are angels who behold the face of God.
They see what Job cannot.
They see what we cannot.
But that immediately raises another uncomfortable question. If guardian angels are watching over us, what does their presence actually mean?
It cannot simply mean that terrible things will not happen.
Job makes that impossible to say.
Terrible things happened to Job. He lost people he loved, his possessions, his health, and almost every security surrounding his life. If the presence of God and His angels meant protection from suffering, Job would be very difficult to explain.
So maybe the Guardian Angels reveal something deeper than the promise that nothing painful will happen to us.
There is more happening than what we can see.
Job is almost the perfect example of this. He could see his suffering, but he couldn't see everything surrounding it. He didn't know about the conversation that opened his story. He didn't know where his suffering was going. He couldn't see the enormous order God was describing when He questioned him.
Yet none of Job's inability to see meant that God had stopped seeing Job.
Psalm 139 seems to sit directly between these readings: God has probed us and knows us. He knows when we sit and when we stand. There is nowhere we can go beyond His presence. Even where we cannot see Him, His hand can still guide us.
And then Jesus gives us another glimpse into something normally hidden from our sight: angels who continually behold the Father's face.
There is something beautiful in that, but also something humbling.
We see so little.
We know what is directly in front of us. We know what hurts. We know what we have lost. We know what we fear and what we hope will happen. From that small piece of reality, we try to understand the whole.
God's questions to Job expose how impossible that is.
And then there is the child in today's Gospel.
The disciples ask Jesus who is greatest in the Kingdom of heaven. Jesus places a child among them. Someone small, dependent, and easily overlooked. Yet Jesus warns them not to despise even one of these little ones because their angels behold the face of the Father.
Job is small before the enormity of creation.
The child is small by the measurements of the world.
But small does not mean insignificant.
Job cannot answer where light lives, yet the God who commands the morning speaks personally to him from the storm.
The child has no worldly greatness, yet Jesus tells us that the child's angel beholds the face of God.
Maybe we are smaller than we imagine and more precious than we understand.
There are still questions these readings don't answer. Why are some people spared suffering while others are not? What exactly are our guardian angels doing when terrible things happen? Why does God allow us to see so little of what He sees?
I don't know.
Job wasn't given all those answers either.
But he was given something.
He discovered that his inability to understand God did not mean God was absent. And today's Gospel opens another window into that unseen reality: heaven is not empty simply because our eyes cannot perceive it.
Not seeing God is not the same as being unseen by God.
There is more happening than what we can see
